It does not explain why a VMM must intercept privileged guest instructions in trap-and-emulate virtualization, so it doesn't help with the conceptual question.

grades.quote: The high-stakes group need not fear consequences from an attacker breaking into the low-stakes group’s system any more than if the two were on different hardware machines. The VMM provides that assurance.
grades.reason: Introduces VMMs and says the VMM isolates virtual machines from one another, which is background for why it needs control. It does not discuss privileged instructions, trapping, or emulation.

grades.quote: The VMM runs in kernel mode. When the underlying processor executes instructions from one of the virtual machines, on the other hand, it does so in user mode. That way, the VMM is in complete control and can protect the virtual machines from one another.
grades.reason: Directly explains the trap-and-emulate mechanism. Guests run in user mode and the VMM runs in kernel mode, so the VMM stays in complete control and can protect VMs from each other. Privileged instructions trap to the VMM, which checks the simulated mode and either carries out the instruction or simulates a trap.

grades.quote: The first is to improve the speed of instruction emulation in a trap handler, partly by allowing the handler to skip loading the trapping instruction from memory, and partly by obviating some of the work of decoding and executing the instruction.
grades.reason: Describes RISC-V H-extension trap information (mtinst/htinst) that helps a trap handler emulate a trapping instruction. This is auxiliary to the question and does not explain why the VMM must intercept privileged guest instructions.
